items.title: Focus Question: Does the speed of a passenger walking down the aisle of a moving airplane depend on your frame of reference?

answer.html: Yes. Positions and velocities depend on the reference frame: for example, a passenger walking at 1 m/s relative to the plane is moving at about 1 m/s relative to the cabin but at roughly 250 m/s relative to the ground. Different observers get different velocities, but the same physical laws apply.

items.title: Figure 13 (Recall): a diagram shows a swimmer's velocity relative to the water and the water's velocity relative to the shore as two arrows. What do the lengths of the arrows indicate?

answer.html: The lengths show the magnitudes (speeds) of the velocities: a longer arrow means a faster speed.

items.title: Get It? (Identify): a swimmer swims in a stream. When would you subtract the swimmer's speed relative to the water from the stream's speed (or the reverse) to find the speed relative to the shore?

answer.html: When the two velocities are along the same line but in opposite directions (for example, swimming upstream against the current), so one is negative and the magnitudes are subtracted. When they point the same way (swimming downstream), the magnitudes are added.

items.title: Physics Challenge: tension in a string (Dara whirls a ball, the string breaks)

question.html: Dara whirls a 0.25 kg ball in a horizontal circle of radius 0.90 m at a height of 1.6 m above the ground. The string breaks when its tension reaches 12 N. (a) Find an expression for, and the value of, the horizontal distance 𝑥 the ball travels before it hits the ground. (b) Does this distance change if Dara is walking at 0.80 m/s in the direction the ball is moving when the string breaks?

body.html: (1) Before the break, the tension is the centripetal force: 𝑇= 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟, giving the speed. (2) After the break, the ball moves off tangentially as a horizontal projectile: constant horizontal speed, fall from rest vertically through ℎ.
𝑥= 𝑣𝑡= √𝑇𝑟

For part (b): relative to Dara, the ball's motion is the same circle with the same tension, so the same expression holds for the distance measured in her frame. Relative to the ground, the ball's velocity at release is the vector sum of its tangential velocity and her 0.80 m/s (they point the same way here), so the ground-frame landing point shifts forward by

answer.html: <sub>𝑚𝑔</sub>= 3.8 m (b) Measured in Dara's frame the distance is unchanged (3.8 m). Measured from the ground, the ball lands 0.46 m farther along her direction of walking, so the ground-frame distance becomes about 4.2 m.

check.html: Units: N · m · m / (kg · m/s<sup>2</sup>) = m<sup>2</sup>, so 𝑥 is in meters. A ball released at 6.6 m/s from 1.6 m up should travel several meters, as found.

items.title: Get It? (Explain): a tick on a cow walking across a field

question.html: Write the equation for the tick's velocity relative to the field.

body.html: 𝑣<sub>a/b</sub> + 𝑣<sub>b/c</sub> = 𝑣<sub>a/c</sub> with a = tick, b = cow, c = field.

answer.html: 𝑣<sub>tick/field</sub> = 𝑣<sub>tick/cow</sub> + 𝑣<sub>cow/field</sub> (vector sum)

items.title: Figure 14 (Analyze): a diagram shows a passenger's velocity relative to a moving train. How would the vector change if the train were considered the stationary frame and the passenger's frame were considered the moving one?

answer.html: It would point in the opposite direction with the same magnitude: swapping the roles of the two frames reverses the relative velocity (𝑣<sub>A/B</sub> = −𝑣<sub>B/A</sub>).

items.title: Get It? (Decide): can a moving train be a reference frame?

answer.html: Yes. Any coordinate system, including one fixed to a train moving at constant velocity, can be a reference frame, and you can state positions and velocities relative to the train.

items.title: Get It? (Describe): how could an airplane in a steady wind stay in one location relative to the ground?

answer.html: The airplane must head directly into the wind with an airspeed (speed relative to the air) equal to the wind speed, so its velocity relative to the ground is zero.

items.title: Get It? (Explain): how are vectors used to describe relative motion in two dimensions?

answer.html: Each velocity is a vector drawn tip to tail (or split into 𝑥 and 𝑦 components); adding the object's velocity relative to the moving frame to the frame's velocity relative to the ground gives the object's velocity relative to the ground.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 25: you walk forward at 1.3 m/s on a moving walkway that moves at 1.6 m/s relative to the floor

question.html: What is your speed relative to the floor?

body.html: Same direction, so velocities add: 𝑣<sub>you/floor</sub> = 𝑣<sub>you/walkway</sub> + 𝑣<sub>walkway/floor</sub>.

check.html: The answer exceeds both given speeds, as expected when moving the same way.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 26: a beetle crawls toward the rear of a toy cart

question.html: The cart moves forward at 0.40 m/s; the beetle crawls 1.50 m/s toward the rear relative to the cart. What is the beetle's velocity relative to the ground?

body.html: Opposite directions, so subtract. Choose forward (the cart's direction) as positive.
𝑣<sub>beetle/ground</sub> = 𝑣<sub>beetle/cart</sub> + 𝑣<sub>cart/ground</sub> = −1.50 m/s + 0.40 m/s = −1.10 m/s

answer.html: about 1.1 m/s toward the rear (opposite the cart's motion)

check.html: The beetle crawls faster than the cart moves, so it ends up moving backward relative to the ground.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 27: a kayak heads upriver at 3.8 m/s relative to the water and moves at 1.1 m/s relative to the shore

question.html: Find the speed and direction of the river's current.

body.html: 𝑣<sub>kayak/water</sub> = 3.8 m/s upriver, 𝑣<sub>kayak/shore</sub> = 1.1 m/s upriver. Find 𝑣<sub>water/shore</sub>.
𝑣<sub>kayak/shore</sub> = 𝑣<sub>kayak/water</sub> + 𝑣<sub>water/shore</sub>. Take upriver as positive.
𝑣<sub>water/shore</sub> = 𝑣<sub>kayak/shore</sub> −𝑣<sub>kayak/water</sub> = 1.1 m/s −3.8 m/s = −2.7 m/s

answer.html: The river flows at 2.7 m/s, downstream (opposite the direction the kayak is heading).

check.html: The current slows the kayak from 3.8 to 1.1 m/s, consistent with a 2.7 m/s opposing current.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 3), Problem 37 (Critical Thinking): a swimmer crossing a river to a spot directly opposite

question.html: A swimmer can swim 1.6 m/s relative to the water. The river flows at 1.0 m/s and is 45 m wide. At what angle upstream from straight across must she aim to land directly opposite her start, and how long does the crossing take?

body.html: To end up straight across, the velocity relative to the shore must have zero component along the river. So the swimmer's velocity relative to the water must have an upstream component equal to the current's speed.
Let the river speed be 𝑣<sub>𝑟</sub>= 1.0 m/s and the swimmer's speed relative to water be 𝑣<sub>𝑠</sub>= 1.6 m/s. Aim upstream at angle 𝜃 from the straight-across direction:
The component across the river carries her to the other bank:

answer.html: She must aim 39° upstream of straight across, and the crossing takes about 36 s. This works only if 𝑣<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝑣<sub>𝑟</sub>; if the river flowed faster than 1.6 m/s it would be impossible to land directly opposite.

check.html: The crossing speed (1.25 m/s) is less than 1.6 m/s because part of her effort fights the current, so the time is longer than the 28 s she would need if there were no current.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: Why does a stream of water from a garden hose curve downward in an arc?

answer.html: Because gravity is the only force on the water after it leaves the nozzle, it gives each drop a constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s², while the horizontal velocity stays constant. Combining the two independent motions gives a parabola. Evidence: the dropped and horizontally launched objects fall together (Figure 2), the calculations for projectiles in Lesson 1 (Problems 1–11), and the softball path below. This supports the claim, so no revision is needed. (The STEM Unit Project is a separate project activity with no data given here.)

(More precisely, 16.1 m. The ball reaches the wall at 𝑡= 𝑥/ 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>= 2.54 s, still above the wall's top. It is descending at that moment, with 𝑣<sub>𝑦</sub>= −6.5 m/s.) The peak of the path is about 18 m above the ground.

answer.html: about 16 m above the ground at the wall (16.1 m)

items.title: 3: Claim.

answer.html: Yes, the hit is a home run (the ball clears the wall).

items.title: 4: Evidence and reasoning.

answer.html: At the wall the ball's height is about 16.1 m, which is about 2.1 m above the 14-m top of the wall. Since the ball passes the wall's distance (96.0 m) while still in the air and above 14 m, it clears the wall. This ignores air resistance, which would reduce the height and range in a real game; a margin of about 2 m is large enough that the conclusion is likely to hold for a modest air-drag effect.
